issues.legal_issue: Compensation for business profits lost during temporary requisition of business premises is a revenue receipt when the business continues and its profit-making apparatus is not destroyed.
material_facts: The business premises included six sheds used to store timber and an office; the sheds were temporarily requisitioned for government use.
The business continued from the office in its usual name and style, although on a smaller scale.
The compensation was claimed and awarded for loss of earnings during the requisition.
The profit-making apparatus was not destroyed, and the business was not permanently deprived of a source of income.
The compensation was calculated as a lump sum using a measure based on two years’ purchases.
issues.conclusion: The compensation was a taxable revenue receipt, not a capital receipt; the method used to calculate the lump sum did not alter its character.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, profits of a business are taxable, and compensation paid in place of profits that would have been earned ordinarily partakes of the character of those profits. The quality and purpose of a payment, rather than the method or measure used to calculate it, determine whether it is capital or revenue. Commissioner of Income Tax/Excess Profits Tax, Bombay City v. Shamsher Printing Press supports treating compensation for lost profits as revenue. Senairam Doongarmall v. Commissioner of Income Tax was distinguished because the business there had stopped completely. The Glenboig Union Fireclay Co. Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue was distinguished because the payment there compensated for sterilisation of a capital asset. The court also held that Commissioner of Income Tax, Nagpur v. Rai Bahadur Jairam Valji, S. R. Y. Sivaram Prasad Bahadur v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Commissioner of Income Tax v. Prabhu Dayal did not apply to these facts.

rule.if: income_tax_reference and premises_temporarily_requisitioned and compensation_awarded_for_lost_business_earnings and business_continued_during_requisition and profit_making_apparatus_not_destroyed and source_of_income_not_permanently_lost

predicates.income_tax_reference: The dispute is before a court in a reference concerning the income-tax treatment of a receipt.
predicates.premises_temporarily_requisitioned: The business premises were taken for temporary use rather than permanently acquired.
predicates.compensation_awarded_for_lost_business_e: Compensation was awarded to replace earnings the business lost during the period its premises were requisitioned.
predicates.business_continued_during_requisition: The business continued during the requisition, even if at a reduced scale.
predicates.profit_making_apparatus_not_destroyed: The business’s profit-making apparatus was not destroyed or sterilised.
predicates.source_of_income_not_permanently_lost: The business was not permanently deprived of its source of income.

issues.definition: When a tax reference concerns compensation for lost business earnings during temporary requisition, and the business continues without destruction of its profit-making apparatus or permanent loss of its income source, the compensation is treated as a taxable revenue receipt.

issues.legal_issue: In a tax reference, the higher court must decide the legal question on the facts found by the tribunal and cannot go behind or reassess those facts.
material_facts: The tribunal found that the business continued from the same office, in its usual name and style, but on a smaller scale.
The respondent challenged the tribunal’s factual findings before the higher court.
The court treated the tribunal as the final fact-finding authority and the statement of facts as binding.
issues.conclusion: The higher court could not go behind the tribunal’s findings and had to decide the referred question on the facts stated by the tribunal.
issues.legal_principle: In a reference under section 66(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, the tribunal is the final fact-finding authority. The High Court and Supreme Court determine the law applicable to the facts found and cannot question or go behind the tribunal’s statement of facts. Karnani Properties Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal was relied on for this principle.

predicates.tax_reference: The proceeding asks a higher court to answer a legal question referred from a tax tribunal.
predicates.tribunal_found_relevant_facts: The tribunal made findings of fact relevant to the legal question referred.
predicates.party_challenges_tribunal_facts_before_h: A party asks the higher court to question or depart from the tribunal’s factual findings.

issues.definition: When a tax reference relies on relevant facts found by the tribunal and a party challenges those facts before the higher court, the higher court decides on the tribunal’s facts rather than reassessing them.
